newsitem.title: USA: Stocks rally with bonds, dollar drops.
newsitem.headline: Stocks rally with bonds, dollar drops.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks surged for a second day in a row Thursday on fresh signs of strength in the technology sector, and bonds firmed on downbeat economic news.
The dollar fell against the Japanese yen and German mark as traders questioned its recent rapid rise.
The 30-stock Dow Jones industrial average ended up 83.12 points at 6,823.86, adding to Wednesday's gain of 85 points, which was its first gain after five sessions of losses.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines 1,543 to 910 on heavy volume of 520 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The market also was relieved that Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan did not come out with any surprises in his second congressional testimony about the economy in less than two weeks.

In prepared testimony before the Senate Finance Committee, the Fed chief gave little hint that the central bank was considering raising interest rates at the Feb. 4 and 5 meeting of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee.
"I still picture them as trigger-finger ready but I don't think it will happen next week," said Allen Sinai, chief global economist at Primark Decision Economics.

Greenspan said that the Consumer Price Index, a leading gauge of inflation, was overstating inflation by 0.5 percent to 1.5 percent, and that he opposed the idea of the federal government becoming a huge shareholder in stocks through the Social Security System.
"If the Fed doesn't raise rates, then there's still upside," said Edgar Peters, chief investment strategist at PanAgora Asset Management Inc.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up nearly half a point, which lowered its yield to 6.87 percent from Wednesday's close of 6.90 percent. The yield and the price move in opposite directions.
Over the last two days the Dow index has recouped two-thirds of what it lost during its five-day skid.
Peters said the recent sell-off might actually be a sign the market was behaving in a more healthy fashion than in recent years.
"The market rose very fast and that was a little crazy," he said. "You have to expect some pullbacks. The thing that's been unhealthy is the lack of pullbacks over the last year or two."
Semiconductor companies were among the strongest performers, boosted by Intel Corp.'s decision to hold prices essentially steady for its high-end Pentium Pro chips in the first quarter.
The dollar ended the day at 121.79 yen, down from 122.18 yen late Wednesday. Against the mark, the dollar settled at 1.6370, below Wednesday's 1.6440.

In commodity markets, oil prices rose as traders focused on expectations of tighter heating oil supplies and colder weather and shrugged off a possible six-month extension of U.N.-authorised Iraqi oil sales.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, February heating oil closed 1.50 cents a gallon higher at 70.34 cents and February unleaded gasoline rose 1.59 cents a gallon at 69.82 cents. March crude closed up 40 cents at $24.87 a barrel.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index ended 20.9 points higher at 4,228.4. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 index dropped by 471.26 points, or 2.57 percent, to end at 17,864.04.
